newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi says it is sticking to reform path.
newsitem.headline: Burundi says it is sticking to reform path.

text.p: Burundi's Tutsi-led military leadership said on Sunday it would stick to its political reforms even if these did not win an immediate end to the sanctions now stalling the country's economy.
"President (Pierre) Buyoya has been clear what his agenda is and he has delivered a lot of promises," said the military ruler's spokesman Jean-Luc Ndizeye.
"He is sticking to that path," he told Reuters.

Buyoya on Friday announced the unbanning of political parties and the restoration of the National Assembly, suspended after he took power in a July 25 coup. But Tanzania reacted by saying that this did not go far enough.
Tanzanian foreign minister Jakaya Kikwete said the sanctions, largely driven by his country, could only be lifted after a full return of parliamentary and constitutional rule to Burundi.
Other conditions for an end to a crippling embargo include talks between the Tutsi-led military government and the Hutu rebels fighting a furious civil war.
The sanctions, agreed by neighbouring African states on July 31, have cut surface and air communications with landlocked Burundi, bringing growing shortages of fuel and other imported goods.

Around 150,000 people have been killed in the last three years of fighting, and regional states fear Burundi could go the way of its northern neighbour Rwanda. In Rwanda up to a million people died in fighting and genocidal massacres of Tutsis and moderate Hutus by radical Hutus in 1994.
Ndizeye said Buyoya's government was now waiting for a response to its offer of talks from the political parties, as well as the rebels.
"We are the dialogue camp," he said, adding that the government was prepared to talk to anyone "as long as they give up killing civilians and reject the ideology of genocide".

Ousted Hutu president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya has been holed up at the U.S. embassy residence since shortly before the coup. Diplomatic sources said Buyoya's government had been in contact with the deposed president's Frodebu party in an effort to ensure their participation in the restored assembly.
Pro-Hutu parties led by Frodebu hold 65 seats while pro- Tutsi parties headed by Uprona occupy 16.
Military officials said there had been incidents of violence outside the capital on Saturday and early on Sunday, but with no reports of any deaths.

Spokesman Lieutenant-Colonel Isaie Nibizi said armed groups had attacked two military posts near Mabayi in northern Cibitoke province, but were repulsed. In Bujumbura province there had been several incidents, but no casualties had been reported and the situation was calm on Sunday, he added.
